headings.title: Introduction to HIV Prevention
headings.content: Prevention of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) infection is a cornerstone of global and national public health nursing, particularly within the Nigerian healthcare framework. HIV remains a significant public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa, making comprehensive understanding of prevention strategies vital for nursing students. Prevention encompasses a spectrum of activities aimed at reducing the risk of acquiring or transmitting the virus. These strategies range from behavioral modifications and biomedical interventions to structural approaches that address social determinants of health, stigma, and gender inequalities. As frontline healthcare providers, nurses occupy a critical position in bridging the gap between scientific prevention methods and community implementation. Understanding the modes of transmission—predominantly unprotected sexual intercourse, mother-to-child transmission, and contact with infected blood or bodily fluids—guides the formulation of effective nursing care plans. By integrating evidence-based prevention modalities into routine clinical practice and community outreaches, nurses actively contribute to achieving the global goal of ending the HIV epidemic. Comprehensive prevention education also empowers vulnerable populations, such as adolescents, key populations, and pregnant women, to make informed health decisions, thereby significantly reducing new infection rates across various healthcare settings in Nigeria.

headings.title: ABCD Prevention Strategy
headings.content: The ABCD prevention strategy is a classic, easy-to-remember framework widely utilized in public health and nursing education to counsel individuals on reducing their risk of contracting HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. 'A' stands for Abstinence, which is the most effective way to avoid sexual transmission of HIV by refraining from sexual intercourse entirely. This approach is frequently emphasized when educating youths and adolescents. 'B' represents Be faithful, encouraging mutual fidelity within long-term, uninfected relationships, thereby eliminating the risk introduced by outside or multiple concurrent sexual partners. 'C' stands for Condom use, highlighting the correct and consistent use of male and female barrier methods during every sexual encounter to physically block the transmission of infectious fluids. Finally, 'D' often stands for Drugs or Delay, referring to avoiding substance abuse that impairs judgment regarding safe sexual practices, or delaying sexual debut among young people. Nigerian nursing students must master the ABCD strategy to effectively conduct health education sessions in antenatal clinics, youth centers, and rural community outreaches. This framework provides clear, actionable steps that empower clients to take control of their sexual health, lower infection rates, and foster healthier lifestyle choices within their respective communities.

headings.title: Biomedical Interventions: PrEP and ART as Prevention
headings.content: Biomedical interventions have revolutionized modern HIV prevention, shifting the paradigm from purely behavioral approaches to powerful pharmacological tools. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) involves the daily use of antiretroviral medications by HIV-negative individuals who are at substantial risk of infection, such as discordant couples or key populations, to prevent acquiring the virus. Nurses play a vital role in screening candidates for PrEP, assessing renal function, providing adherence counseling, and monitoring for potential side effects. Another groundbreaking biomedical concept is Treatment as Prevention (TasP), which relies on Antiretroviral Therapy (ART). When an HIV-positive person takes ART consistently and achieves an undetectable viral load, they cannot sexually transmit the virus to an HIV-negative partner. This principle is famously summarized as Undetectable equals Untransmittable (U=U). For nursing students, understanding TasP is crucial because it helps combat internalized and societal stigma against people living with HIV (PLHIV), while also emphasizing the therapeutic benefit of viral suppression. Nurses must advocate for unhindered access to antiretroviral drugs in Nigerian healthcare facilities, educate patients on the absolute necessity of medication adherence, and provide continuous support to ensure long-term viral suppression and community-level protection.

headings.title: Universal Precautions in Clinical Settings
headings.content: Universal precautions, now commonly integrated into standard precautions, are a set of infection control practices designed to protect healthcare workers and patients from exposure to bloodborne pathogens, including HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C. The fundamental principle underlying universal precautions is that every patient's blood and body fluids, secretions, and excretions (except sweat) should be treated as potentially infectious, regardless of their known serostatus. Key components of universal precautions include meticulous hand hygiene before and after patient contact, safe handling and disposal of sharps in puncture-resistant containers, and the appropriate use of personal protective equipment (PPE) such as gloves, gowns, face masks, and eye protection whenever exposure to bodily fluids is anticipated. Furthermore, nurses must exercise extreme caution to avoid needle-stick injuries, which remain one of the highest occupational risks in clinical environments across Nigeria. Recapping of used needles is strictly prohibited; instead, syringes with safety devices or immediate disposal into designated safety boxes must be practiced. Environmental controls, such as proper decontamination of spilled blood with chlorine solutions and correct sterilization of surgical instruments, are equally paramount. Nursing students must cultivate these habits diligently during clinical postings to foster a safe healing environment for both themselves and their patients.

headings.title: Post Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)
headings.content: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) is an emergency biomedical intervention designed to prevent HIV infection following a potential occupational or non-occupational exposure to the virus. Examples of exposures include needle-stick injuries in clinical settings, unprotected sexual assault, or broken skin contact with infected bodily fluids. For PEP to be effective, it must be initiated as soon as possible—ideally within 2 hours of exposure, and no later than 72 hours—since delayed initiation significantly decreases its efficacy. The standard regimen typically involves a combination of two to three antiretroviral drugs taken consistently for a duration of 28 days. When a nursing student or clinical staff member experiences a needle-stick injury, immediate first aid is mandatory: the wound should be washed gently with soap and running water (without scrubbing or bleeding the wound aggressively), and the incident must be reported immediately to the infection control unit or occupational health nurse. Following the report, a risk assessment is conducted to determine the necessity and specific regimen of PEP. Emotional support and baseline HIV testing for the exposed individual and, where feasible, the source patient, are integral parts of the protocol. Nurses must understand PEP protocols thoroughly to act promptly during emergencies and provide empathetic guidance to traumatized or anxious patients.

headings.title: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT)
headings.content: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT) encompasses a comprehensive cascade of interventions aimed at halting the transmission of HIV from an infected mother to her child during pregnancy, labor, delivery, or breastfeeding. Without interventions, the risk of vertical transmission ranges from 15% to 45%, but with a robust PMTCT program, this rate can drop below 5%. The PMTCT continuum begins with routine, voluntary HIV counseling and testing (HTC) for all pregnant women attending antenatal care (ANC) clinics. If a mother tests positive, lifelong ART is initiated immediately, regardless of her CD4 count, to achieve viral suppression. During labor and delivery, healthcare providers practice safe obstetric techniques, avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures such as artificial rupture of membranes or episiotomies when avoidable. Following birth, infant prophylaxis with syrups such as nevirapine or zidovudine is administered, and early infant diagnosis (EID) using DNA PCR testing is performed at strategic intervals. Infant feeding counseling is another vital nursing responsibility; mothers are guided on either exclusive replacement feeding (if acceptable, feasible, affordable, sustainable, and safe) or exclusive breastfeeding while adhering strictly to maternal ART and infant prophylaxis. By implementing these measures meticulously, nurses play a transformative role in eliminating pediatric HIV infections in Nigeria.

headings.title: Community Education and Nursing Roles in HIV Prevention
headings.content: Community education and advocacy are foundational elements of nursing practice that extend HIV prevention efforts beyond hospital walls into neighborhoods, schools, religious centers, and rural settlements. Nurses serve as educators, counselors, and change agents who combat pervasive myths, misinformation, and stigma associated with HIV. Stigma remains a formidable barrier to testing, treatment adherence, and disclosure; therefore, nurses must lead destigmatization campaigns by promoting compassionate, non-judgmental care and educating communities on the actual routes of transmission. Community outreach programs led by nurses often involve distributing educational materials, organizing free voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) camps, demonstrating correct condom use, and linking diagnosed individuals to care hubs. Furthermore, nurses advocate for policy changes, gender equality, and the protection of vulnerable groups, recognizing that social inequalities heavily influence HIV vulnerability. Empowering young girls and women through economic and educational initiatives is also highlighted during community sessions, as structural drivers frequently intersect with biological risk. By fostering open dialogue and creating safe spaces for discussion, nursing students and professionals build resilient communities capable of supporting prevention programs, reducing new HIV infections, and improving overall health outcomes across Nigeria.
